extraction.name: HELVIPAD
extraction.description: HELVIPAD is a real-world dataset for omnidirectional stereo depth estimation, featuring 40K video frames from 29 video sequences captured in diverse environments, including crowded indoor and outdoor scenes with various lighting conditions (day and night). Collected using two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup with a 19.1 cm baseline and an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor, the dataset includes accurate depth and disparity labels by projecting 3D point clouds onto equirectangular images. An augmented training set with increased label density via depth completion is also provided.
extraction.creator: Mehdi Zayene, Jannik Endres, Albias Havolli, Charles Corbière, Salim Cherkaoui, Alexandre Kontouli, Alexandre Alahi (EPFL, Switzerland; TU Darmstadt, Germany)
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data were collected using a custom-built rig equipped with two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a vertical (top-bottom) arrangement with a 19.1 cm baseline, capturing equirectangular images at 30 fps, paired with a synchronized Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor with a vertical field of view of 42.4°, operating at 10 fps, mounted 45.0 cm below the bottom camera. A central NVIDIA Jetson Xavier processor managed data capture and synchronization. The rig was mounted on a custom-built, remotely controlled robot chassis. 29 video sequences were collected across a university campus, capturing pedestrian activity in indoor (corridors, halls) and outdoor (squares, parking, footpaths) settings under various lighting and weather conditions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Physical data collection, Direct measurement, Experiments
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: LiDAR point clouds are sparse compared to high-resolution camera images, with ground-truth depth labels covering only ~12% of total pixels before depth completion. Occlusions were not explicitly handled, as the small LiDAR-camera baseline minimizes their impact.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of equirectangular images from two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras (initial resolution 3840 × 1920 pixels at 30 fps) and 3D LiDAR point clouds from an Ouster OS1-64 sensor (64 beams, 10 fps, 42.4° vertical field of view), collected on a university campus.
extraction.rai:dataImputationProtocol: A fully automated depth completion pipeline was developed for 360° images. It uses temporal aggregation of 9 point clouds (4 preceding, current, 4 succeeding), interpolates depth values on a spherical grid via weighted k-nearest neighbors (k=17) in spherical coordinates, and applies filtering based on uncertainty (relative weighted variance with RIP=0.8) and an out-of-distribution threshold (~0.37°) to exclude points without sufficient nearby measurements. This increases the ratio of labeled pixels from 12% to 61%.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: LiDAR point clouds were projected onto equirectangular camera images through an optimization-based mapping algorithm. Key 3D points were selected from a 19x19 chessboard, initial rotation/translation transformations were applied to align the camera lens as the coordinate center, then points were converted to spherical coordinates and projected onto the equirectangular plane. Rotation and translation parameters were optimized via BFGS by minimizing error between projected points and corresponding image pixel positions. Disparity values were computed from depth using the spherical disparity formula.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images and depth/disparity maps were cropped to remove unnecessary regions (sky, ground) and downsized from a width of 1024 pixels to 512 for efficient training, resulting in a final resolution of 1920×512 pixels. Frames were subsampled to match the LiDAR's 10 fps frame rate (retaining one of every three camera frames). Hardware-triggered flash synchronization was used to align camera and LiDAR data streams.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Depth and disparity labels were generated automatically by projecting LiDAR 3D point clouds onto equirectangular camera images using an optimized LiDAR-to-image mapping algorithm. An augmented training set with higher label density was created via automated depth completion. Manual point selection was used for quality assessment of projection alignment.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Projection accuracy was evaluated by manually selecting corresponding points between projected LiDAR data and images, computing Euclidean pixel errors. Average pixel error across the dataset is 8.0 pixels (0.40% of image diagonal); for 200 randomly selected points, error was 1.7 pixels on average. Depth completion pipeline quality was evaluated through 80-20 train-test splits of each LiDAR point cloud with metrics including MAE, RMSE, MARE, and Inlier Ratio.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Custom LiDAR-to-image mapping algorithm with BFGS optimization; custom depth completion pipeline using temporal aggregation and weighted k-nearest neighbor interpolation on spherical grids; KISS-ICP was evaluated but not used for final temporal aggregation.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset captures pedestrians (humans) in university campus environments. Sequences contain an average of 13.33 pedestrians in indoor sequences and 17.65 pedestrians in outdoor sequences. No explicit demographic information about pedestrians is collected.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset was collected on a single university campus, which may limit diversity of scenes. Night outdoor sequences are underrepresented compared to daytime outdoor and indoor sequences (only 2 night outdoor train sequences vs. 13 outdoor and 5 indoor). Models trained on specific environments show limited generalization, particularly indoor-trained models struggling with outdoor scenes at night.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Depth completion via temporal aggregation is limited for fast-moving objects like cars due to the assumption of negligible motion over the 9-frame window. The dataset is limited to a university campus setting. LiDAR provides sparse point clouds, especially for far-range objects. The depth completion pipeline does not provide labels for pixels at object boundaries due to ambiguity. Maximum LiDAR-camera de-synchronization is 16.67 ms. The LiDAR's vertical field of view of 42.4° limits the region with potential depth labels.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing of omnidirectional stereo depth estimation models. Benchmarking stereo matching methods for both standard and omnidirectional imaging. Evaluating robustness of depth estimation methods to diverse lighting conditions and depth ranges. The dataset is split into a train-val set (20 sequences, 29,407 frames) and a test set (6 sequences, 10,146 frames).
